title: The Epidemic of AI and Data centers in relation to Human right to Clean Air or Sustainable environment.
author: Nwanguma Rosemary Chinonso
excerpt: Have you ever found yourself around 2 am, going down the rabbit hole of online research about AI, the complex system that is most likely to replace humans in various key sectors of the economy.
content:
The Epidemic of AI and Data centers in relation to Human right to Clean Air or Sustainable environment.  
The Human rights perspective on Data centers. 
 
Photo by Kevin Ache on Unsplash  
 
 
 
 
Have you ever found yourself around 2 am, going down the rabbit hole of online research about AI, the complex system that is most likely to replace humans in various key sectors of the economy. Well, welcome to the club and if you have not, you are also welcome. Now coupled with your research, you would have probably figured out that these AI systems are heavily dependent on Data centres built all over the world to power them and these structures serve as AI’s physical infrastructure. Side notes: there are approximately about 12,259 operational data centres in the world,  with 93 of them operating as specialised AI Data centres and which according to Bain & Company  the number is speculated to triple by 2030 as many countries are in a race to catch up to overwhelming need of AI compute as against economic survival or dependency with the US toppling the race hosting about 74% of these specialised data centres s compute capacity and China significantly behind with 14%.   
Now with the groundwork laid, It is pertinent to note that with these infrastructures or Data centres, which are becoming a very vital key aspect of the world’s economy (with Bain & Company estimating that as of 2030 the US would have spent  a major chunk  of the globally projected $6.5 trillion spend on this data centres more than construction of rail roads, telecom and electrical grids etc.), are also becoming detrimental and are constituting a violation of human right to clean and sustainable environment which is recognised by the United Nations General Assembly.  
 In order to build a data centre or to sustain it several factors must be taken into consideration like the massive electricity, the cooling, heat, noise pollution, all of which if not well taken into consideration ends up affecting the down end of the chain which are humans who are supposed to benefit. In the city of Mansfield, Georgia, one homeowner Beverly Morris complains of polluted water, an excerpt from BBC Correspondents (Michelle Fleury & Nathalie Jimenez) interview “I’m afraid to drink the water, but I still cook with it, and brush my teeth with it,” says Morris. “Am I worried about it? Yes.” Morris who bought her dream home in 2016 hoping to enjoy it with her once beloved front porch, came to regret that decision, when Meta owned by Facebook built a data centre close to her beloved spot. Morris has complained that since then her well water supply has been contaminated by residue which she claims are from the Data centre, in which Facebook has denied all allegations. Morris is one of the many residents affected by these Data centres located close to their homes or communities.  It is estimated according to the Environmental and Energy Study Institute (EESI) that it takes about 5 million gallons per day to quench the thirst of Data centres which is equivalent to a town of 10,000 to 50,000 people.  The resulting effect of data centre quenching it thirst might be water insecurity, dehydration, and poor hygiene for so many others who do not even have enough water. 
In another city of Bristow, Virginia, one resident is heard complaining of the noise from Google’s “Mango Farm” Data centre, US News Correspondent, Cecelia Smith-Schoenwalder, who covered the story, an excerpt from the interview, “As somebody who has anxiety, it triggers an anxiety attack in me every time they’re doing load testing, to the point where I can’t sleep because it literally rocks your core,” Gallant says. Donna Gallant like so many of her neighbours who moved to Williams County about 30 years ago, which she described the state as once “quiet” and “beautiful” has become in her words “an Industrial Wasteland”. Gallant has had to take extreme measures by replacing her windows because of the sound which still penetrates her home from the Google’ “Mango Farm” Data centre.

According to a 2025 study made about the effects of Data centres on society.  It was discovered that gas powered data centres emit significant pollutants such as nitrogen oxide, methane, volatile organic compounds and fine particulate matters, and that these pollutants increase the rate of respiratory diseases, cardiovascular conditions and cancer risk among nearby communities. It is also estimated according to a 2025 model that by 2030 the US would have spent a total of $20 billion as resulting effect of a public health crisis which could cause 600,000 asthma symptoms cases and 1,300 premature deaths.  
In 2022, the United Nations General Assembly fully recognised the right to clean and sustainable environment as a universal human right after long years of scholarly discourse about this topic, which had left many apprehensive. This recognition came as a result of long-standing climate advocacy which started from the 1972 Stockholm Declaration, and which has lasted to this century.  During the 2022 resolution, Inger Andersen had this to say, “This resolution sends a message that nobody can take nature, clean air and water, or a stable climate away from us – at least, not without a fight”. In response to this resolution many countries like the UK, Cyprus, India and so many others have adopted it in their framework.  
 Mind you, Long before the adoption of this Resolution in 2022 many countries have recognised and adopted the right to clean air and sustainable environment in their frameworks, For example In Nigeria, Section 20 of the Constitution of the federal Republic of Nigeria (as amended) and National Environmental (Air Quality Control) Regulations, 2014 in Regulation 1(b) recognise, this right.  However, in Nigeria and so many other countries, what has been burdensome has been the level of implementation due to either ineffective enforcement bodies or none at all as the case may be. 
 Having explored this right and seen that its major barrier is its lack of proper implementation, which the AI and the Data centre industry use to their benefit.  How then can we balance the scale so that the uprising of AI and Data centres do not lead to the end of the Human race and the end of free flow information (Article 19 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights).  I say this in the sense that this Data centre consumes a massive amount of basic human essentials like Water, Electricity, Land and so on. It is therefore should be a prerogative to balance AI’s needs and Human needs. 
It is in this regard that I  recommend that each country should have a regulation that governs AI and Data centre industry, that limits/specifies how many to build in a time frame and an independent body free from external interference, that takes a critical look at submission to build data centres from each industry and that takes into consideration the human rights and available resource to satisfy such. 
In conclusion, Data centres are necessary but when they stand to expose humans to more dangers than benefit, it is necessary that a balance be struck such that human right to sustainable environment is prioritised but doesn’t impede technological progress, access to information or economic growth.

title: From Shanbaug to Rana: Judicial Law Making on Euthanasia in India and the Need for Legislation.
author: Nishalya Singh
excerpt: Euthanasia, derived from the Greek words ‘eu’ meaning “good” and ‘thanatos’ meaning death signifies the intentional administration of a lethal agent to a patient for the purposes of relieving the patient of their prolonged suffering.
content:
From Shanbaug to Rana: Judicial Law Making on Euthanasia in India and the Need for Legislation. 
Euthanasia, derived from the Greek words ‘eu’ meaning “good” and ‘thanatos’ meaning death signifies the intentional administration of a lethal agent to a patient for the purposes of relieving the patient of their prolonged suffering. Euthanasia therefore can only be administered in cases where the patient has been in a vegetative state with no scope for improvement and the patient’s survival is only subject to the continued assistance of life support systems. The law surrounding Euthanasia has been controversial due to its moral ramifications and often the courts have wrestled with the issue of interpretation of such an equivocal law. While advocates for this law on one side argue for its implementation with the broader view of the right to having a dignified death, the opposition argues with the moral ramifications of allowing an individual to be allowed to die, making the issue more morally grey. Furthermore, there are two types of Euthanasia central to the scholarly discussions that have taken place, Active and Passive Euthanasia. Active Euthanasia is when specific actions are taken on purpose to end an individual’s life, whereas Passive Euthanasia is the withdrawal of life support mechanisms which would allow the patient to die peacefully. Thus, this research paper intends to ask several questions, Whether Article 21’s scope includes the right to a dignified death, Whether the Aruna Shanbaug case and the Common Cause case can be used for interpretive guidance on Euthanasia cases and Whether India’s current legal stance on Euthanasia needs a novel change. 
The case of Aruna Shanbaug 
Aruna Shanbaug, a 24-year-old nurse at King Edward Memorial Hospital faced a brutal assault, following which she was left in a permanent vegetative state and the staff of KEM took care of her for nearly four decades. In 2009, the journalist Pinki Virani, who had written a book on Aruna’s life filed a petition under Article 32 to the Supreme Court to request for removal of life support since her constant treatment violated the right to live with dignity. The respondent KEM hospital contended that Ms. Shanbaug was duly fed and cared for by the nurses and the hospital has been taking utmost care and responsibility in maintaining the patient’s health and they would like for her to pass naturally. They contended that since the caretaking was primarily done by the hospital, they would be the guardians and thus had the authority to decide if Aruna should undergo Euthanasia . The Petitioners on the other hand contended that Aruna, being in a permanent vegetative state was essentially under extreme agony, having no scope of getting better and being in the same state of suffering for the last 36 years. The Supreme Court followed the principle of ‘parens patriae’ and bestowed powers upon the court to ultimately decide in the best interests of the patient, by also giving due weight to the views of near relatives, next friend and doctors. The court ultimately decided against the administration of Euthanasia, by concluding that Aruna Shanbaug was capable of showing some brain activity and that the decision of the KEM Hospital staff should be respected considering they were the primary caretakers of Aruna Shanbaug for the last four decades. Thus, the case laid down several guidelines for allowing Passive Euthanasia, and recognised it as a facet of Article 21, relying on the judgement passed in the case of Gian Kaur v. State of Punjab  acknowledging the prolonged suffering and indignity faced by individuals in a permanent vegetative state, emphasizing that the decision to withdraw life support should be made by the High Court. 
The Scope of Article 21 and the Common Cause case.

Article 21 of the Indian Constitution states that “No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.” Thus, Article 21 of the Indian Constitution establishes the fundamental rights of Right to Life, Privacy, Livelihood, Dignity, Medical Care, Education and a Clean and Healthy environment. Among these rights, The Right to a Dignified Death is one that is most wrestled with by the Courts, believing it to be included within the fold of Right to live with Dignity, protected by Article 21. whenever a case involving Euthanasia has come for adjudication. 
To further understand the stance of the courts, we look at the case of Common Cause v. Union of India . In this case, there was a petition filed seeking to expand the “right to life” under Article 21 of the Indian Constitution to include the right to die with Dignity, treating it as an inseparable and inextricable facet of the right to live with dignity. The Court here reaffirmed that the right to die with dignity is a fundamental right. In the words of the Court, “Constitutional recognition of the dignity of existence as an inseparable element of the right to life necessarily means that dignity attaches throughout the life of the individual. Every individual has a constitutionally protected expectation that the dignity which attaches to life must subsist even in the culminating phase of human existence. Dignity of life must encompass dignity in the stages of living which lead up to the end of life. Dignity in the process of dying is as much a part of the right to life under Article 21. To deprive an individual of dignity towards the end of life is to deprive the individual of a meaningful existence.” This landmark verdict serves as a turning point in recognizing the Right to die with Dignity as an intrinsic facet of the Right to live with Dignity. Furthermore, the court addressed the distinction between Passive Euthanasia and Active Euthanasia, stating that Active Euthanasia entails the positive act or act of commission involving the use of lethal substances to cause the intentional death of another person, whereas Passive Euthanasia entails the withdrawal of life support measures for continuance of life. The Right to Privacy was further discussed by the Courts, bringing the Right to deny medical intervention or treatment as an integral facet of the Right to Privacy. The Court stated, “The principle of sanctity of life thus recognises the fundamental liberty of every person to control his or her body and as its incident, to decline medical treatment.” Additionally, the phenomenon of a ‘living will’ was recognised by the Supreme Court of India, recognising the individual’s choice to undergo Euthanasia at a later stage if the individual is unfortunately in a vegetative state.   
Another judgement which gives further clarification upon the stance of the courts on Euthanasia is the case of Harish Rana v. Union of India . After being in a vegetative state for a period of 13 years following a brain injury, parents of Mr. Harish Rana filed a petition in the Supreme Court for allowing the administration of Passive Euthanasia to their son, in order to relive him of his prolonged suffering and so he could die naturally with dignity. The Supreme Court for the very first time allowed for the administration of Passive Euthanasia. The Supreme Court laid down that Clinically Assisted Nutrition and Hydration is a medical treatment that can be withheld or withdrawn, even when administered in a home setting. Secondly, Withholding and withdrawal of medical treatment, the term preferred over ‘passive euthanasia’, means respecting the dignity of the patient and letting the natural course of death happen.  Thirdly, the process is only applicable for persons in a vegetative state or terminal illness like conditions. It is put into operation when (a) the patient loses decision making capacity and (b) further treatment would be considered futile.

Finally, the court recommended that the Union Government consider enacting comprehensive legislation on the subject. Thus, the guidelines set out by the Supreme Court in the Common Cause case were applied to their complete extent. Justice Chandrachud’s opinion in the Common Cause case was that the “best interest’ has to be balanced with the substituted judgement standard as a matter of “public interest”. In the present case, the Court added that both the Primary and Secondary Medical Boards had stated that the Withdrawal of Clinically Assisted Nutrition and Hydration treatment was in the best interest of the patient. It clarified that the Court is not always the final arbiter when it comes to determine the welfare of the patient. Towards the end of his opinion, Justice Pardiwala stated that the decision was not an “act of surrender” but one of “compassion and courage”.  It was not rooted only in logic and reason but “sits in a space between love, loss, medicine and mercy.” Acknowledging the emotional weight that the decision carried, Justice Pardiwala addressed Rana’s parents directly, stating “you are not giving up on your son, you are allowing him to leave with dignity. It reflects the depth of your selfless love and devotion towards him.” 
Does the current framework require a novel change? 
The cases discussed so far show that India’s law on Euthanasia has been built almost entirely by the Judiciary, by expanding the scope of Article 21 to include the Right to Die with Dignity as an intrinsic facet of the Right to Live with Dignity. While the present framework has made commendable achievements, by describing the withdrawal of life support as the withholding or withdrawal of medical treatment, rather than as passive euthanasia, and by holding that clinically assisted nutrition and hydration is a medical treatment, Harish Rana answered the objection that had led the Delhi High Court to dismiss the petition In 2024, namely that the removal of a feeding tube is considered starvation and would be in substance active euthanasia. This reasoning is consistent with the approach taken by the House of Lords in Airedale NHS Trust v. Bland , which also treated artificial nutrition as medical treatment. The Court also made clear that withdrawal must be accompanied by palliative care and that families and doctors who act in accordance with the procedures are not subjected to criminal liability under the BNS, 2023. There are however weaknesses in the framework which also need to be addressed in order to advocate for a stronger change. 
Firstly, the absence of an enacted statute makes the issue meticulous, as the courts often take prolonged periods of time to adjudicate upon an issue. In the Harish Rana case, the Delhi High Court dismissed the father’s petition in 2024, after his son’s fall in the year 2013. The Supreme Court constituted the medical boards in 2025 and delivered the judgement in March 2026. Few people have the resources to litigate up to the Supreme Court and the fact the Court had to direct the High Courts to prepare Judicial Magistrates for intimations and the Union to ensure that panels of doctors exist, suggests that the machinery put in place by the 2018 guidelines have not been placed uniformly since the last eight years in which they were issued. The Law Commission of India recommended a Bill on the medical treatment of terminally ill patients in its 196th Report (2006) and revisited the subject in its 241st Report. The Health Ministry circulated a draft Bill in 2016 and draft guidelines on the withdrawal of life support in 2024. The fact that no law has yet been passed entails consequences upon the legality of withdrawing treatment, which still rests on Judicial guidelines, while the BNS continues to penalise culpable homicide and murder (Sections 100 and 101) and abetment of suicide (Section 108).

Thus, judicial guidelines can protect those that follow in the instant, however they do not amend the penal statute and a doctor or family who is uncertain of if a particular case falls within the respective ambit of Euthanasia may choose to continue treatment rather than risk prosecution.  
 If the Right to Die with Dignity is to be more than a right on paper, the procedure must be made accessible without undergoing prolonged litigation, and the Right to a Dignified Death must be matched by access to palliative care so that the Right to Live with Dignity is not conditional upon a family’s wealth. 
Thirdly, the distinction between active and passive euthanasia on which the entire framework rests is difficult to defend as a matter of grave moral implication, since in both cases, the intention is for the patient to be relieved of their suffering. The framework allows this only where the patient is incapable of decision making or is terminally ill or in a vegetative state, and where treatment would be futile. As inferred, a patient who is suffering unbearably from an illness deemed incurable, but who is not dependent on any treatment that can be withdrawn has no lawful route to Euthanasia and can only be offered palliative care. This raises the question whether Parliament should go further and legalise active euthanasia or physician assisted dying, as the countries such as the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg, Spain and Canada have done, as the US state of Oregon has done in the form of assisted dying with the Death with Dignity Act enacted in 1994   , and as Switzerland has partly done by tolerating assisted suicide . Jurisdictions that permit active Euthanasia have built extensive regulatory framework for eligibility criteria, independent assessment and review, and even they continue to debate whether eligibility should be widened. India has not built the foundation upon which such a system could rest safely. 
Conclusion: 
International Jurisprudence on Euthanasia is evolving, and India must engage in a transparent, evidence-based discourse on its ethical, medical and legal aspects. India can ensure that its legal system stays humane, pertinent and effective in protecting the rights and dignity of individuals at the end of life only by doing so. Euthanasia should not be reduced to a binary of life and death. It raises an ethical and legal question that requires careful analysis of personal autonomy, medical ethics, societal values and statutory protection. The Indian Legal System possess the capacity to establish an international benchmark for reconciling these conflicting interests and safeguarding the dignity and rights of its citizens, especially those who wish to live and die with Dignity.

title: When Imitation Isn’t Infringement: Dupe Culture and the Limits of Trade Dress Law
author: Sanskrati Jain
excerpt: Browsing through any social media platform lately will make you a witness to one recurring theme: “run, don’t walk” to some place that is selling a dupe of a luxury or premium item at a significantly lower price (Lamendola, 2026).
content:
When Imitation Isn’t Infringement: Dupe Culture and the Limits of Trade Dress Law
Browsing through any social media platform lately will make you a witness to one recurring theme: “run, don’t walk” to some place that is selling a dupe of a luxury or premium item at a significantly lower price (Lamendola, 2026). Influencers hold the two items next to each other, openly claiming the cheaper one to be a copied dupe. It may be a bargain and a better purchase for consumers, but it poses a legal issue for brand owners, many of these issues turning into litigation. Lululemon’s suit against Costco, which targets Kirkland-label athleisure and several other third-party brands the wholesale store sells, is one of the better known (Reed Smith, 2025). Questions have arisen in court regarding whether deliberate imitation and its marketing are matters of trademark and advertising law (The Fashion Law, 2025). Is it really deception if a copy is marketing itself as a copy?
The aim of trade dress law is to give credit to the person making the product, not to give any person the ownership of any specific style of clothing. Protection has conventionally been awarded to the source, not resemblance, and dupe litigation risks stretching the doctrine beyond that.
Section 43(a) of the Lanham Act provides the owner of an unregistered trade dress the right to sue where a similar design is likely to cause confusion among consumers regarding the origin of the product (15 USC § 1125(a)). It was held by the US Supreme Court that product design is never inherently distinctive, so the claimant must prove that consumers associate a particular design with one source (Wal-Mart Stores v Samara Brothers, 2000), and that monopoly cannot be exercised over functional features (TrafFix Devices v Marketing Displays, 2001; 15 USC § 1125(a)(3)). Indian law has a similar view through passing off, which requires goodwill, damage and misrepresentation. The Delhi High Court has asked repeatedly whether trade dress is the overall appearance through which consumers identify a product’s origin (Colgate Palmolive v Anchor Health, 2003; Cadbury India v Neeraj Food Products, 2007). Indian law limits design protection, with protection for unregistered designs ending after more than fifty industrial reproductions (Copyright Act, 1957, s 15(2)). Trademark registration is limited as well in the case of the shape of goods and colour combinations if these characteristics achieve a technical result, result from the nature of the goods or add substantial value to them (Trade Marks Act, 1999, ss 2(1)(zb), 9(3)).
The legal dispute between Lululemon and Costco gives an idea of the issue at hand. Lululemon filed a suit in a California federal court, alleging that Costco’s Kirkland athleisure clothing is a copy of some of Lululemon’s signature pieces such as the Scuba hoodies and the Define jacket along with its signature ABC pants (Reed Smith, 2025). The suit also covers other brands that Costco sells, including Hi-Tec, Jockey, Spyder and Danskin. The matter is that of trade dress, design patent and trademark law. These claims have not been proven yet, and it has been reported that the majority of the claims have since been settled out of court in 2026 (Bloomberg Law, 2026).
Lululemon is not attempting to claim a logo, since Costco’s garments do not have one. Lululemon is claiming to own a seam line (triangle seam), a colour name (Tidewater Teal), federal trade dress registrations and two design patents on the Scuba hoodie. These are characteristics that buyers would perceive as a style and not something signature to a brand. A court allowing this would enable a monopoly that goes beyond a label and into mere details that are necessary for the production of any item.
An Indian court would perceive such a dispute as passing off, questioning whether a regular consumer would confuse the two products as being from the same source. A consumer who goes into Costco knowing which product comes from Kirkland does not fit that test easily.

In Sol de Janeiro v MCoBeauty, a dispute over fragrance-mist packaging, the defendant argues that the features claimed are functional, generic and not distinctive, and that its comparisons to the original are lawful and not deceptive (The Fashion Law, 2025). The argument has weight at the point of sale: a consumer seeking to buy a dupe is not deceived about the source. Brands’ arguments focus on onlookers rather than buyers, stating that part of the dupe’s value lies in how it is perceived when seen in public, where it might be confused for the original. This is post-sale confusion, which is concerned with source and not just prestige. The UK Supreme Court in Iconix v Dream Pairs [2025] UKSC 25 held that post-sale confusion can be perceived as infringement even without any confusion at the point of purchase. The case, since it concerns only registered trademarks, offers limited support to brands, holding persuasive value in India and the US. The doctrine has been questioned by US scholars as well, with Powell (2012) contending that it is unnecessary in a market where the existence of knock-offs or dupes is well known to consumers, while Raustiala and Sprigman (2018) arguing that post-sale confusion may be real, but a rare occurrence, causing no real harm to a brand’s reputation or status. Consumers are not deceived by dupes, and it must be proven that a significant number of onlookers are confused or deceived to establish liability.
A clearer comparison is visible under design law rather than trade dress when like is set against like. The EU protects against deliberate imitation for three years from first disclosure (Regulation (EC) No 6/2002, arts 11 and 19, as amended by Regulation (EU) 2024/2822). An unregistered design in India has no enforceable rights, relying instead on passing off, which requires goodwill, or on copyright, which ends after a design has been industrially reproduced more than fifty times (Copyright Act, 1957, s 15(2)). Registered designs in India are given a ten-year protection with a one-time five-year extension (Designs Act, 2000, s 11), while the EU provides a twenty-five-year protection in renewable terms of five years (art 12). The EU provides a true head start with its three-year term where the maker gets an opportunity to establish distinctiveness, while India gives no similar opportunity; an unregistered designer has to rely on consumer confusion.
Brands make a fair argument that an identity built over years of investment is being free-ridden. At the same time, the head start is given to original designs for this very reason: to make their designs distinctive enough to the consumers such that, even if they are being copied, a buyer knows the source of the design. Expanding trademark or design law to protect a design that is generally considered a style would risk a monopolistic market infringing consumer rights.
Three limits exist. Dilution, which does not depend on confusion, and comparative advertising, which governs how dupes are marketed, deserve separate treatment. The claim that dupe buyers are not deceived is empirical. This is arguable, not proven, for the lack of evidence.
A dupe is not a fraudulent copy: it does not deceive the buyer at the point of sale; on the contrary, it flatters the original. Courts should limit the scope of trademark law to counterfeits and refrain from broadening it to dupe products. Resemblance cannot be made actionable: fashion would lose the momentum of borrowing and reworking that it thrives on, and consumers would be left with limited options.

title: Diplomatic Immunity During Armed Conflict: Syria and the Limits of State Responsibility
author: Adwaith Sinoop Devan
excerpt: The article examines how the Syrian conflict has exposed gaps in diplomatic immunity under the Vienna Convention, particularly through the 2012 embassy closures and the 2024 Israeli strike on the Iranian consulate in Damascus. It highlights the challenges of enforcing state responsibility during armed conflict and proposes reforms to strengthen diplomatic protection.
content:
Abstract  
The Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations 1961 is clear, unqualified, that inviolability of diplomatic premises and persons exists “even in case of armed conflict.” Fourteen years of violence in Syria have put that assurance to the test in situations the Convention's framers could not have foreseen: a receiving state given "little control" over its territory, a series of unilateral embassy closures, and a third-state military strike on a consular building, resulting in the deaths of top foreign military officers. This article explores the Syrian conflict's culmination the Israeli attack on the Iranian consulate in Damascus on 1 April 2024 and the structural imbalance between the text-based absolute rights of diplomatic immunity and the comparative weak construction of state responsibility to enforce it. The article concludes that the law of diplomatic immunity was designed for an inter-state setting in which collapse of the state and third-party involvement outrun it, each in its own fashion, as they both have in the cases of the Tehran hostages, Nicaragua and Bosnian genocide, respectively. It brings the three modest, treaty-external reforms that can help reduce the attribution and enforcement gaps that the Syrian conflict has exposed.

Keywords  
Diplomatic immunity; Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations; state responsibility; Syria; armed conflict; attribution; non-state actors.

. Introduction  
Syria has gone from a functioning (although autocratic) state to a broken land divided between a central government, various armed opposition groups, jihad groups and foreign militaries since March of 2011. The injury has posed a direct threat to one of international law's most established and ancient regimes: that of diplomatic immunity. The inviolability of a mission's premises and immunity of its personnel continue to exist "even in case of armed conflict," as stated explicitly in the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations 1961 (“VCDR”).  Later generations of diplomats simply took this for granted, as a reminder that the niceties of international life don't just disappear when the shooting starts. That has become a question in the Syrian conflict, one that is alive and often hotly debated.  
The inquiry that follows is preceded by two episodes. First, since February to June 2012, over a dozen states, including the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada and the Gulf Cooperation Council monarchies, closed their embassies in Damascus and removed their diplomats.  They didn't say the regime has expelled them, but rather the “bad security situation and the repression of protesters. Second, and far more spectacularly, on 1st April 2024 Israeli planes bombed a building having the consular section of the Iranian embassy in the Mezzeh district of Damascus, killing seven members of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, including high-ranking officials.

Less than two-weeks later, a direct attack by the Iranian drone and missile forces on Israeli territory was reported, which was condemned by a majority of the UN Security Council,  and dubbed by the UN Secretary-General as a violation of a principle that must be respected “in all cases”.  The episode proves that violations of diplomatic immunity are not simply treaty matters of “housekeeping” but can be a proximate cause of other military conflicts between states.

In this article, the author contends that the Syrian case illustrates a structural fault line between the textbook certainty of diplomatic immunity and the rather underdeveloped historical framework of state responsibility to enforce it. The VCDR speaks little of what is to take place if the receiving state, or its territory, loses the effective control that the sending state has over it; it speaks little of what is to take place if a third state, which has no direct treaty relations with the sending state's mission, strikes a diplomatic compound from the air. Part II outlines the legal framework for the treaties. Part III then considers the international law of state responsibility, specifically the attribution of state's responsibility on the basis of the Articles on the Responsibility of States for Internationally Wrongful Acts (“ARSIWA”)  of the International Law Commission and the approach of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) to the concepts of due diligence and control. In Part IV, it is applied in a critical way to Syria, comparing and contrasting the 2012 closures and the 2024 Damascus strike; Part IV also addresses the unique challenge posed by non-state armed actors. Part V provides with three recommendations outside the confines of the treaties, and Part VI ends.

II. The Treaty Architecture of Diplomatic Immunity in Armed Conflict
 
Less than two weeks later, a direct attack by the Iranian drone and missile forces on Israeli territory was reported, which was condemned by a majority of the UN Security Council, and dubbed by the UN Secretary-General as a violation of a principle that must be respected “in all cases”. The episode demonstrates that violations of diplomatic immunity are not simply treaty matters of "housekeeping" but can be a proximate cause of other military conflicts between states.

The VCDR speaks little of what is to take place if the receiving state, or its territory, loses the effective control that the sending state has over it; it speaks little of what is to take place if a third state, which has no direct treaty relations with the sending state's mission, striking a diplomatic compound from the air. Part II outlines the legal framework for the treaties. Part III then considers the international law of state responsibility, specifically the attribution of state's responsibility on the basis of the Articles on the Responsibility of States for Internationally Wrongful Acts (“ARSIWA”) of the International Law Commission and the approach of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) to the concepts of due diligence and control. In Part IV, it is applied in a critical way to Syria, comparing and contrasting the 2012 closures and the 2024 Damascus strike; Part IV also addresses the unique challenge posed by non-state armed actors, whereas Part V provides with three recommendations outside the confines of the treaties, and Part VI ends.

III. State Responsibility: Attribution and the Due Diligence Standard  
If the VCDR is silent, it is assumed that the general law of state responsibility will come into play (Welcome to United Nations, “Vienna Conventions on Diplomatic Relations, 18 April 1961”). Adopted by the International Law Commission in 2001 and generally considered to reflect customary international law, ARSIWA states that an internationally wrongful act occurs when a state's act is attributable to such state and is in violation of an international obligation of that state.  In cases where the behaviour is that of an Office for State Services, attribution is normally easy.  Where the physical perpetrators are private individuals, militias or armed groups loosely affiliated with a government, it becomes much trickier; a situation that has been the rule since 2012 throughout much of Syria.

The ICJ's decision in United States Diplomatic and Consular Staff in Tehran is the key precedent for a receiving state's duties to a mission threatened by non-state actors.  On the evidence before the Court, the Court determined that the initial seizure of the US embassy by militant students could not be attributed to Iran as the exercise of the state per se. Even if it had not acted to prevent, end, or force the militants out of Iran, which is also a duty under the VCDR, Iran's government, which had already acted in such a way in the past, ended up, in the public reaction to the attack, by endorsing the occupation and turning it into an act of the state.  
The Tehran Hostages thus creates two separate lines of responsibility which are applicable to Syria: a separate due diligence obligation, which a receiving state has even if the attack itself is carried out by another state; and a doctrine of ex post facto adoption (which, more recently, was reflected in Article 11 of ARSIWA, a rule of attribution under which a state's subsequent acknowledgment and adoption of otherwise-private conduct as its own makes it responsible for that conduct as if it were the state's own.

In the case of attribution based on relation to an armed group in the first instance, there are two approaches in the case law. The ICJ in Military and Paramilitary Activities in Nicaragua determined that Nicaragua must establish “effective control” of the particular activities in which the alleged violations took place before the conduct of those activities could be considered to be a part of U.S. involvement in the situation. This requirement was not satisfied by financing, training or even planning support alone, the Court ruled.  The Appeals Chamber at ICTY  rejected this as an unrealistically high bar for organised armed groups, suggesting that an “overall control” test would be adequate to meet the requirement, even if it does not specify a particular violation.  The ICJ looked back into the Bosnian Genocide case and upped the ante on the state-responsibility approach, determining that the “effective control” test continues to be the applicable one for State responsibility, while the overall control test is relevant only to deciding whether foreign control makes an internal armed conflict international for the purposes of humanitarian law.  This unresolved tension is directly relevant for the case of Syria, where many foreign and domestic patrons fund armed factions with differing levels of coordination, and where a strike against a diplomatic mission by any group affiliated with a patron but not directly commanded by it could either or not be blamed on the patron based on the test that an eventual tribunal uses.

IV. Critical Analysis: Syria as a Stress Test 
 
A. Mission Closures, 2012: Due Diligence in a Collapsing State 

By early 2012, the closures were the result of poor security and threats to diplomatic personnel. On 6 February 2012, the United States closed their embassy in Damascus and removed Ambassador Robert Ford and staff from the country due to safety concerns after car bombings in Damascus,  while the United Kingdom followed suit. Formal relations between the United States and Syria were never suspended, and the British embassy suspended its operations on 1 March 2012, while Saudi Arabia and other Gulf Cooperation Council countries withdrew their ambassadors on 7 February 2012 and closed their embassies in Damascus on 15 - 16 March 2012. By the end of 2012, the majority of Western states stopped any in-person operations in Damascus and some Arab states stopped as well.

On their face, these closures were voluntary, rather than expulsion by Syria, but rather an exercise of the sending states' prerogative. But they shed a different light on due diligence in Tehran Hostages. So long as the receiving state's protective capacity is clearly and overtly weakened, as is the case in countries where missions have been targeted by bombings, mobs near embassies, or an internal security set-up that is engrossed in repression, the protection of the premises of the mission, as prescribed in Article 22,  becomes practically untrustworthy, irrespective of its formal status. The sending states' reaction was not to take legal and/or diplomatic actions to claim the responsibility of Syria, but to simply walk away without attempting to establish whether or not Damascus could still comply with its duties under the Vienna Convention. That seems like a reasonable answer to the question that is of great doctrinal interest: Is the disappearance of a receiving state's security guarantee suspends its VCDR obligations or simply makes them unenforceable? To date, the answer has been almost entirely theoretical, with only a handful of limited applications in practice. ARSIWA doesn't accommodate a slow-moving unable state: its force majeure clause requires that performance be “materially impossible,”  an exceedingly high standard that an able-bodied state facing an internal threat, but still running along the outside, will seldom satisfy on its own. The outcome is a paper commitment that becomes increasingly irrelevant as a system of accountability. That is the place that Part V will get back to.

The principle of Article 45 did not fare as well on the severance of relations,  although public record on individual compounds is too sparse to draw conclusions on compliance in any specific case. By mid-2012, it was obvious that a state receiving a repertoire of embassies in a capital that was increasingly plagued by violence deemed itself to have sufficient administrative resources to safeguard dozens of embassies scattered across the city, and that assumption was in tension with reality.

B. The Damascus Consulate Strike, April 2024: A Third-State Problem 
The best example of the structural weakness of the VCDR is not Syria's, but a third state's. Israeli aircraft bombed a building that was part of the Iranian embassy compound in the Mezzeh district of Damascus on 1 April 2024 killing seven people including high-ranking commanders of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). The Vienna Conventions, which guarantee the immunity of diplomatic and consular premises, have been denounced by Iran, Syria, Russia and China,  the latter stating that any encroachment on diplomatic and consular buildings is “completely unacceptable” by the foreign ministry. A majority of the members of the UN Security Council condemned the attack at an emergency session of the Council called by Russia, and the Secretary-General reiterated the principle of inviolability mentioned above.  On 13 April 2024, Iran retaliated by directly attacking Israeli territory with drones and missiles,  which were significantly neutralised by Israel and its partners. The exchange is a good example of the direct link between the violation of a special diplomatic immunity and open inter-state confrontation.

The strike creates a doctrinal conundrum that the 2012 closures do not. Article 22 VCDR is deeper entangled than it first seems, and it is not Israel, but “the receiving State” – Syria – that is bound to the Convention. Several commentators have tried to link the loss-of-protection doctrine, which forms a component of humanitarian law, to the current strike, claiming that the same principle should apply to a diplomatic facility hosting or coordinating the military activities of an organisation like the Quds Force as to a hospital in wartime. This analogy isn't really one to take on board. The VCDR is not a document of international humanitarian law, and there is no textually drafted exception to the protection of civilians in the document similar to the ‘conditional protection'  granted to medical facilities in the Geneva Conventions. On the contrary, its protection for the premises of the missions is expressed in the same unconditional register as the rest of the Convention, namely the “even in case of armed conflict” formula. However, if an IHL forfeiture concept is imported into a treaty regime expressly designed to lack such a concept, then a particular protection that the drafters of the treaty considered essential and inescapable may be deemed to be lapsed by the third state on the basis of its own view of the use of the mission. The diversity of international condemnation indicates that most governments have not yet reached the point of embracing the desired outcome as positive law, despite the many governments that may have had a fleeting sympathy for the security rationale behind it.

A more coherent frame would focus on the strike as being chiefly about the territorial sovereignty of Syria and the jus ad bellum, not the diplomatic rights of Iran as such: whether the building was military or civilian, Article 2(4) of the UN Charter would be implicated,  and the diplomatic nature of the building target would make the wrongfulness of the underlying use of force more, not less, evident. On this approach, the VCDR does not itself create a stand-alone immunity to third-state attack; the special gravity of such attacks, as a matter of customary international law's general respect for the inviolability of such premises, as reflected in the almost-uniform state condemnations, is more properly characterized as the general rule of customary international law than a treaty right that can be asserted directly against a third state under a bilateral instrument limited to receiving and sending states.

The Attribution Gap and the role of Non-State Armed Actors. 

Add a third dimension to the problem. The territory of the Syrian state has been home to an unusually high concentration of non-state armed groups since 2013, from the Islamic State to a string of opposition groups with varying degrees of foreign support, who could, in theory, strike at a diplomatic mission or members of a diplomatic mission. The question of responsibility, if any, would largely depend on the interpretation of Nicaragua's “effective control” test and Tadić's “overall control” test, both of which were discussed in Part III, in the event of such an attack and in the event that a victim state sought to hold a patron state responsible. The ICJ's more stringent effective control test, which the court reaffirmed in the Bosnian Genocide case  as the test for state responsibility, would reapplicability to cases of financing, training, and provision of matériel, without necessarily directing individual operations, would leave many potential cases of patron-proxy relationships unchallengeable for attribution if a State provides material support to a group in question. The practical effect is that, in the vast majority of realistic scenarios, an attack on a diplomatic mission by a non-state group active in Syria might not be remediated in terms of state responsibility because it is not attributable to the state nor indeed to a foreign patron, but rather can only engage the responsibility of the non-state actor itself, which is not part of the ARSIWA regime.

V. Recommendations 

The following three reforms would help to close the gaps listed above. None of them necessitates reopening of the text of the VCDR.  
States and international organizations should work to establish, through regular practice and public declaration, a distinct and separate from, and more stringent than, the VCDR, rule which expressly prohibits military operations by third states on diplomatic and consular premises, regardless of the receiving state's ability to protect them. The near-uniform condemnation of the Damascus strike in April 2024,  even from states which were not aligned to Iran, indicates that the normative material for such a rule is already available, it is only a step to consolidating it into a statement by a body like the International Law Commission or as UNGA resolution or as ICJ advisory opinion.

Second, the due diligence obligation that was expressed in Tehran Hostages should be specifically modified in later state practice or in scholarly statements to deal with diminished or compromised state competence, not allowed to become the all-or-nothing test of Article 23's more rigorous standard of force majeure.  A tiered standard, under which a receiving state experiencing serious loss of territorial control would still be bound to take "protective and facilitative measures" that are within its actual power, and to cooperate with sending states in good faith in order to ensure their own withdrawal and the safekeeping of their archives, would follow the events in Damascus between 2011 and 2012 more closely than the binary of full compliance and impossibility. 
Third, in view of the lack of consensus in politically divided bodies like the Security Council to enforce diplomatic sovereignty, states or regional organisations should take greater advantage of the advisory powers of the ICJ and of fact-finding mechanisms under the residual powers of the General Assembly to establish an authoritative and reasonably up-to-date factual and legal record of attacks on diplomatic premises in the context of the Syrian conflict.  For any future bilateral claims, this would matter and for the project of consolidation of the customary rule suggested above.

VI. Conclusion
 
In Syria, the Vienna Convention's guarantee of the survival of diplomatic immunity, in "even in case of armed conflict," has been mostly honored in theory rather than in practice, but it remains so. As showed by the 2012 closures, a receiving state's responsibilities may be difficult, if not impossible, to enforce as soon as its governmental capacity begins to decline. The strike on the Iranian consulate in Damascus in April 2024 was more pointed: the attacks on diplomatic premises, especially those of third states, are condemned as a matter of general international law and intra- state political solidarity, but are not redressed as a matter of treaty right, in the bilateral structure of the VCDR. For many realistic attacks on diplomatic missions, none of the states with interests in Syria may be held responsible under existing tests of attribution, in light of the density of non-state armed actors operating throughout the Syrian territory since 2013. None of this constitutes failure on the part of the VCDR; its fundamental prohibitions still exist and still are considered by the vast majority of States to be law, for as the response to such a strike in Damascus is proof, the VCDR was not part of any state's action. However, Syria has demonstrated, with unusual transparency, the text-absolutist nature of the Convention, which was designed for the inter-state paradigm that has both been outstripped by a collapsing state and by an interventionist neighbour. The task of filling that gap lies with the law of state responsibility, and the customary international law. It cannot be expected to be achieved only by Vienna Convention.

title: Beyond the Bounds of Marriage: Re-Thinking Section 498A in the Age of Live-in Relationships
author: Vanshika Singla
excerpt: In Dr. Lokesh B.H. v. State of Karnataka (2026), the Supreme Court extended Section 498A IPC to certain live-in relationships resembling marriage, provided the required legal conditions are satisfied. The judgment seeks to strengthen protection against domestic cruelty while raising concerns about judicial interpretation, criminal liability and the boundaries of personal relationships.
content:
Case citation: Dr. Lokesh BH v State of Karnataka 2026 INSC 784 (SC, 3 August 2026) (Karol and Kotiswar Singh JJ)

FACTUAL BACKGROUND 
The issue began as a matrimonial argument. Smt. Theertha alleged that she married Dr. Lokesh B.H. by Hindu rites on 17 October 2010, both lived in Bengaluru together and eventually fell out in 2016.  Later two complaints were filed producing charge-sheets under section 498A of the Indian Penal Code 1860 (IPC) and in another sections 504, 506, 307 and 494 IPC and the Dowry Prohibition Act 1961.  The FIR alleged that he concealed an earlier marriage, demanded dowry and injured her, leaving burns on her leg.  Dr. Lokesh denied the existence of any marriage and claimed that he was nobody’s ‘husband’ and section 498A could not apply. 
The Karnataka High Court refused to quash the FIR and interpreted the term ‘husband’ purposively: a man who induces a woman to believe she is lawfully married to him cannot plead the invalidity of the union to escape liability for cruelty.

ISSUES BEFORE THE COURT 
The appeal turned to answer three questions- 
i. Does ‘husband’ in section 498A, now section 85 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS), require a legally valid marriage? 
ii. If not, can a live-in partner fall within it, and on what threshold? 
iii. And does the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005 (DV Act) already cover field, making any extension unnecessary?

DECISION AND RATIONALE 
Karol J, writing for the Bench, rejected the argument that a penal provision must be confined to a husband in a valid marriage. The court said that, “Strict construction is not strict literalism”  the section’s reformative purpose must shape its reading.  The court’s reasoning in Reema Aggarwal was subsequently endorsed by a three-judge Bench in Rajinder Singh, while Shivcharan Lal Verma was distinguished in its approach and limited to the specific facts of its case.  
The court distinguished between live-in relationships generally and those that have the essential characteristics of a marriage. While the former is a broad category, the latter constitutes a narrower class assessed using the indicators stated in Indra Sarma.  The application of Section 498A accordingly depends on whether the relationship satisfies the relevant legal requirements, with the woman bearing the initial burden of establishing the necessary facts.   Further the court clarifies that the Domestic Violence Act (DV Act) being a civil save for section 31 could not substitute for the criminal deterrence of section 498A.  Distinguishing married from marriage-like couples had no rational nexus with preventing domestic violence and was in contravention with Article 14 . Court emphasized on strict application of Arnesh Kumar safeguards, the extension was confined to section 498A, and quashing was refused because concealment and cruelty were issues that could be answered in the trial.

CRITICAL ANALYSIS 
Reema Aggarwal has limited applicability as it concerns men who enter a marital relationship under the colour of such proclaimed or feigned status of a husband . Its reasoning may not extend to partners who never claimed or were believed to be legally married. The facts in Lokesh BH involved a woman allegedly married through customary rites to man who concealed his existing marriage, the appeal could have been decided on that basis alone. This court’s broader ruling on live-in relationships therefore went beyond what was necessary to decide the case, especially when this concept had limited judicial attention.

Fair warning- Strict construction exists so that people know what criminal before any action is taken. Parliament knew the expression ‘relationship in nature of marriage’ well enough to use it in the DV Act, yet re-enacted ‘husband’ as it is in section 85 BNS.  The “mischief rule” was designed to fills gaps in a statute, not to add classes of accused the legislature may have intentionally left out.  The argument that interpretation merely declares what law always meant, sits uneasily with a construction not previously held by the Supreme Court, and with the fair-notice rationale of article 20(1), which provides protection from punishment under laws not in force at the time of the act.

“Intent to marry” is hard to prove. This is the weakest yet the most original part of the judgement. The Indra Sarma factors already look at the couple’s intention and how they presented themselves.  “Intent to marry” makes the case depend on what the man’s private thought are. The woman must prove that and the man has every reason to deny it. Pranav Mittal warns that a man with an earlier marriage can say this proves he never meant to marry her which takes us back to the defence the court to tried . What matters in a deception case like this one is what the man had conveyed to her and what was reasonably believed by her and not his secret intention. A test based on those two things would be fairer and easier to prove.

Choice, but only for those who want to marry- The Court iterates that people have the right to choose their partner and asks why protection should be different for married and unmarried couples.  However, protection to couples who chose not to marry is denied due to the intent requirement which leaves them with the DV Act’s civil remedies. This is the kind of distinction the court criticised under article 14, only one step down.

Equality used to widen the punishment. The amicus curae relied on Hiral Harsora, where the Court struck down the phrase “adult male” in section 2(q) of the DV Act, so that women could also be respondents.  There the Court removed had removed the limit, here it widens an offence to cover a new section of accused. Widening a civil remedy and widening the scope of a crime are not the same, because the latter can cost a person their liberty. The Court in awareness of this laid down the intent requirement but did not exclusively discuss this.

IMPLICATIONS 
There are three effects that follow. Firstly, the partner’s family. If “husband” now includes a live-in partner, “relative” must include his relatives too, even though U Suvetha held that a girlfriend is not a relative.  Parents and siblings can be accused, and court also worries elsewhere in the judgement about families being dragged in . Secondly,  there are limits, the judgement only covers section 498A, so section 304B IPC which provides for dowry death, which Reema Aggarwal also dealt with, stays outside its scope.   Thirdly, the judgement likely invites substantial disputes in court. Accused will challenge “intent to marry” at the threshold, leaving it to the trial courts to contend with the evidentiary standards required to establish it. Whether the judgement strengthens women protection or only leads to more arrests will depend on the extent to which the police follow the safeguards laid in Arnesh Kumar guidelines of 2014.

CONCLUSION 
This judgement addresses a genuine concern. A man should not get to escape a cruelty charge merely because a marriage ceremony was invalid or did not take place, and civil remedies alone are insufficient. The Court’s verdict says that no live-in partner or relative should be arrested without a preliminary inquiry. However, the solution the court provided still creates a new judicial category altogether, resting on a state of mind that is hard to prove, and placed on a provision that Parliament re-enacted without any changes in 2023. A better approach would have been to decide the case on Reema Aggarwal and the man’s own representation of his intent leaving the question of unmarried partners to the Legislature. The ruling does widen the law’s reach but leaves its boundaries to be settled case by case.

title: MMDR Amendment Act, 2026: States Plan Supreme Court Challenge Over Mineral Taxation
author: Chhavi Agarwal
excerpt: The MMDR Amendment Act, 2026, has triggered a federalism debate, with Karnataka, Kerala and Telangana planning to challenge its restrictions on states’ mineral taxation powers before the Supreme Court.
content:
Date:- 20 August 2026 
Location: New Delhi

Lead: Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh has announced that Karnataka, Kerala and Telangana will challenge the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Act, 2026, before the Supreme Court, citing concerns over states’ taxation powers and fiscal autonomy. No petition had been filed at the time of the announcement.

Background: In Mineral Area Development Authority v. Steel Authority of India (2024), a nine-judge Bench held, by 8:1, that royalty is not a tax. It held that states’ power to tax mineral rights under Entry 50, List II is subject to limits set by Parliament by law relating to mineral development, but that these limits do not apply to taxes on land, including mineral-bearing land, under Entry 49, List II.

Key Developments: Parliament passed the Bill on 12 August in the Lok Sabha and on 13 August in the Rajya Sabha. The President assented on 17 August 2026. The Act restricts state levies on mineral rights and mineral-bearing land, subject to conditions prescribed by the Central Government. It also deems every tax, cess or levy on such rights or land that the state had not received or recovered before commencement “invalid at all material times”, while barring refunds of amounts already deposited or recovered. It comes into force on a date notified by the Central Government.

Legal Significance: PRS Legislative Research accepts that Parliament may limit state taxes on mineral rights under Entry 50, but questions its competence over mineral-bearing land, which falls under Entries 18 and 49, List II. It also questions the retrospective invalidation of dues and the delegation of conditions to the Central Government, and raises an Article 14 concern: companies that did not pay are relieved of their dues, while those that paid receive no refund. The Central Government maintains that the legislation promotes uniformity in mineral taxation. The constitutional validity of the Act remains open to judicial scrutiny.

title: Supreme Court Stays Gujarat HC Proceedings on Deepfake Regulation
author: Chhavi Agarwal
excerpt: The Supreme Court has stayed proceedings before the Gujarat High Court in a PIL seeking a regulatory framework for AI-generated deepfakes, while considering the Centre’s plea to transfer the case. The matter raises important questions about intermediary liability, digital platform accountability and the regulation of AI-generated content in India.
content:
Date | Location:8 September 2026 | New Delhi

Lead: By an order dated 8 September 2026, the Supreme Court stayed proceedings beforethe Gujarat High Court in a public interest litigation (PIL) seeking a regulatory frameworkfor AI-generated deepfakes. The order was passed while the Court considered the UnionGovernment’s petition seeking the transfer of the matter to the Supreme Court.

Background: The PIL, filed by Vikas Vijay Nair, seeks a broader regulatory framework toaddress the misuse of artificial intelligence in creating and circulating deepfake photographsand videos, particularly those targeting constitutional and statutory authorities. By an orderdated 10 April 2026, a Division Bench of the Gujarat High Court comprising Chief JusticeSunita Agarwal and Justice D. N. Ray issued notices to Meta, Google, X, Reddit and Scribd,seeking their responses to the petition. The Court also directed the platforms to integratewith the Centre’s SAHYOG portal to facilitate coordinated enforcement and the immediateremoval of unlawful online content

The Union Government and the State of Gujarat highlighted the existing legal frameworkunder the Information Technology Act, 2000, and the Information Technology(Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, as amended in 2026.The Centre also raised concerns about delays and non-compliance by certain intermediariesin responding to takedown notices.

Key Developments: A three-judge Bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant andJustices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana issued notice on the Union Government’s transferpetition and directed that further proceedings before the Gujarat High Court remain stayed.The Union submitted that similar proceedings before other High Courts had already beenstayed and were pending before the Supreme Court. The notice on the transfer petition wasmade returnable on 5 October 2026. The Gujarat High Court’s case status, accessed on 10October 2026, lists the PIL for further proceedings on 27 October 2026.

Legal Significance: The order does not determine whether India requires separatelegislation specifically regulating deepfakes. Instead, it concerns the transfer of the pendingproceedings to the Supreme Court, potentially facilitating the consolidated consideration ofrelated legal issues and reducing the risk of inconsistent judicial approaches. The order mayalso help ensure consistent judicial treatment of related petitions, while leaving the merits ofthe regulatory questions open. uestions concerning intermediary liability, compliance withexisting IT laws, and the need for additional regulatory measures remain unresolved by thisinterim order. The stay pauses the Gujarat High Court proceedings but does not, by itself,suspend the existing statutory framework.

The eventual decision on the transfer petition may influence how Indian courts address theregulation of AI-generated content, the responsibilities of digital platforms, and the balancebetween preventing online misuse and protecting lawful expression

title: DPDP Act–RTI Conflict: Supreme Court Seeks Centre’s Reply on Challenge to Section 44(3)
author: Chhavi Agarwal
excerpt: The Supreme Court is examining whether Section 44(3) of the DPDP Act, 2023, unfairly restricts the public’s right to access information under the RTI Act, 2005. The case raises a crucial question of balancing the right to privacy with transparency, accountability and freedom of speech.
content:
Date | Location:
7 August 2026 | New Delhi
Lead: The Supreme Court has sought the Union Government’s response to petitions challenging Section 44(3) of the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023, which allegedly weakens the Right to Information (RTI) Act, 2005, by restricting access to personal information.
Background: Section 44(3) of the DPDP Act, 2023 substituted Section 8(1)(j) of the RTI Act, which governs the disclosure of personal information held by public authorities. The petitioners, including the RTI activist Venkatesh Nayak and The Reporters’ Collective Trust, argue that the amendment expands the exemption and removes important safeguards for public-interest disclosures. They state that this could undermine transparency, accountability and investigative journalism. The earlier framework balanced privacy against public interest, as examined by the Supreme Court in CPIO, Supreme Court of India v. Subhash Chandra Agarwal (2019), reported at (2020).
Key Developments: In February 2026, the Supreme Court issued a notice on the challenges and declined to stay the amendment and referred the matter to a larger Bench. On 7 August, a Bench comprising Chief Justice of India, Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana granted the Union Government two weeks to file its response. The Court raised the question of whether a blanket restriction on disclosure was permissible or whether a proportionate approach was necessary or not.
Legal Significance: The case raises important questions regarding balancing data privacy with transparency and the right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a). The petitions also invoke Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution. It will examine whether data protection legislation can restrict access to information under an existing transparency law. The Court has not yet ruled on the constitutional validity of the amendment, which remains in force pending further orders.
Next Steps: The matter is to be listed on a non-miscellaneous day after the Union files its response.
